title: The Seven That Remained
note: Narration for the Crownfall: Aethelgard opening. Lines are the creator's text from the revised story concept (The Eighth Oath). Lines marked "added" carry the creator's King's Gambit note (each house may only field certain champions; Ealdholt only pawns; a queen can come from another house) and wait for the creator's approval. "say" is how the voice should pronounce a line when it differs from the subtitle. "pause" is the silence after the line, in seconds.

lines.text: Every kingdom remembers the Hollow King.
Some call him the last true sovereign. Others deny there was ever a throne.
Yet every surviving chronicle speaks of his disappearance.
No tomb was found. No successor was acknowledged.
And in the silence he left behind, men began claiming what they believed had once belonged to him.
Thirty-three years ago, the Sovereign Crown shattered.
The world was divided by ash, ambition and the shards of a broken power.
The Scavenger Wars followed.
Four great powers endured: Korvenia, Solforiz, Kwind-09...
lines.say: Four great powers endured. Korvenia. Solforiz. Kwind Oh-Nine.

lines.text: And Aethelgard.
A land of ancient mountains, immense forests, and seven families who believed that blood alone gave them the right to govern.
The Blood-Throne belonged to seven Great Houses.
One commanded the armies. One guarded the winter grain. One controlled the roads and trade.
One forged the weapons. One preserved the laws and the blood registries. One held the dangerous frontiers.
And the eldest among their rivals claimed dominion over the ancient First-Born.
Together, the Seven swore to preserve Aethelgard.
lines.say: Together, the Seven swore to preserve Ethelgard.

lines.text: But each believed the others unworthy of ruling it.
Long before the houses built their fortresses, the First-Born haunted these lands.
Some were colossal predators. Whole settlements vanished beneath their wings.
Then one Great House proclaimed it had discovered the means to master them.
The people rejoiced.
No longer would the beasts devour their children. No longer would the roads belong to monsters.
Yet few were permitted to ask how such creatures had been brought to obedience.
Or why the price of protection grew heavier every year.
The Seven promised order.
But in Aethelgard, a man's ancestry could decide where he lived, whom he married, whether his children inherited his name, and whether his words were believed before a court.
lines.say: But in Ethelgard, a man's ancestry could decide where he lived, whom he married, whether his children inherited his name, and whether his words were believed before a court.

lines.text: Those without recognized bloodlines were expected to serve the very houses that denied them protection.
Then the Seven turned upon one another.
Accusations became executions. Executions became reprisals.
And every house declared its own violence necessary for peace.
The King's Gambit offered another way to settle the claims of nations and houses.
Sixteen living representatives against sixteen.
But no house may send whomever it pleases.
By the law of blood, only the Seven may raise knights, bishops and rooks.
A queen may be lent from one great house to another, to seal a marriage, or a debt.
Houses whose blood the registries will not recognize, Ealdholt among them, may raise only pawns.
To field a full board, they must borrow from the Seven. And the Seven never lend without a price.
By the judgment of the board, men could win land, passage, custody, and the right to govern.
A contest of law instead of the slaughter of armies.
But the board could declare only a victor.
It could not teach the defeated how to accept defeat.
And in Aethelgard, every judgment became another reason for hatred.
lines.say: And in Ethelgard, every judgment became another reason for hatred.

lines.text: Now the Seven prepare for another war.
Each claims the throne. Each claims to defend the kingdom.
And somewhere within the histories they have guarded lies a truth that could destroy them all.
You are not one of the Seven.
You command no great army. You inherit no ancient privilege.
You have only a banner, a handful of people, and the decisions that will become their history.
In Aethelgard, such things are easily forgotten.
lines.say: In Ethelgard, such things are easily forgotten.

lines.text: Unless you give the kingdom a reason to remember.
